newDescription:
In this Year 4 English term-starter lesson, pupils revisit key grammar, punctuation, reading comprehension and spelling skills. They distinguish questions from exclamations and choose the correct question mark or exclamation mark. They then write descriptive sentences about a tiger, using an expanded noun phrase, the preposition “inside”, a fronted adverbial and an exclamation sentence.

This lesson includes:
✔ Distinguishing questions from exclamations and using question marks and exclamation marks correctly
✔ Writing four descriptive sentences about a tiger, including an expanded noun phrase, the preposition “inside”, a fronted adverbial and an exclamation
✔ Reading “The Labourer’s Wealth” and answering comprehension questions using evidence from the passage
✔ Exploring vocabulary, including the meaning of “profusion”, and considering the author’s choice of “bazaars” rather than “markets”
✔ Adding the suffixes -ous, -ation and -ly to root words, including noticing spelling changes
✔ Identifying expanded noun phrases and writing descriptive sentences of their own
✔ Identifying statements, commands, questions and exclamations, with appropriate capital letters and punctuation
✔ Completing a short research challenge about the average length of a saltwater crocodile
✔ Using apostrophes in contractions and to show singular and plural possession
✔ Recognising contractions and writing their full forms
✔ Spelling words with the “ay” sound using the patterns ei, eigh and ey

Pupils practise suffix formation through examples such as mountainous, courageous and dangerous; adoration, information and preparation; and comically, usually, finally and completely. They identify expanded noun phrases in sentences and consider how describing words and prepositional phrases add detail.

The reading comprehension work is based on “The Labourer’s Wealth”. Pupils answer questions about Abdul Karim’s reaction to receiving money and the present he intends to buy first, then explore the meaning of “profusion” and the author’s use of the word “bazaars”.

The apostrophe activities cover contractions such as can’t, couldn’t, didn’t and it’s, as well as possession for one person and for more than one person. The final spelling activities practise the “ay” sound in words including vein, weight, they, sleigh, neighbour, prey, eight, neigh, freight and grey.

Across the lesson, pupils revisit sentence construction, vocabulary, comprehension, word formation, punctuation, apostrophes and alternative spellings of the “ay” sound.
